title: Text Adventures - The World of Word Processing
subject: ICT
chapter: 11. Text Adventures - The World of Word Processing
description: A comprehensive review of word processing concepts from Text Adventures - The World of Word Processing, covering Microsoft Word and Google Docs basics, creating and saving documents, text formatting (bold/italic/underline), fonts and sizes, alignment, lists, pictures, tables, spelling and grammar checks, find and replace, page formatting, and the history of writing tools from ancient manuscripts to the cloud era.

questions.question: What is word processing, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Word processing is defined in the worksheet as using a computer programme to create, edit, save, and print text documents.
options: Using a computer programme to create, edit, save, and print text documents
Using a typewriter to type letters

questions.question: Microsoft Word's icon is usually shown as a:
questions.explanation: The chapter describes Microsoft Word as having a blue "W" icon.

questions.question: Google Docs can only be accessed when you're connected to the internet.
questions.explanation: Since Google Docs works through the internet in a browser, you need an internet connection to access it, as stated in the worksheet's true/false answer key.

questions.question: Which of these is a word processing program named in the chapter besides Microsoft Word and Google Docs?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists WordPad (and LibreOffice Writer) as other common word processing programs.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an advantage of word processing over handwriting, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Word processing requires a computer and electricity to work, so "requires no electricity" is false — it is actually a limitation of word processing, not an advantage.
options: You can move sentences around without rewriting
You can save your work digitally
It requires no electricity to operate

questions.question: One key benefit of word processing over handwriting is that you can:
questions.explanation: The worksheet answer key confirms word processing is better than handwriting because you can fix mistakes easily without erasing.

questions.question: Which of the following are word processing programs mentioned in the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter names Microsoft Word, Google Docs, WordPad, and LibreOffice Writer as word processing programs. Photoshop (image editing) and Excel (spreadsheets) are different types of software.

questions.question: Google Docs stores your documents:
questions.explanation: Google Docs works through the internet, saving documents online so they can be reached from any connected device.
options: Online, so you can access them from any device
Only on one computer's hard drive

questions.question: Because Google Docs works in a web browser, you never need an internet connection to open or edit your documents.
questions.explanation: This is the opposite of what the chapter states: the worksheet confirms you can ONLY access Google Docs when connected to the internet, since it is a browser/online-based program.

questions.question: According to the chapter's "Trail Treasure" fact, an early word processing machine released in 1964 was called:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Trail Treasure box notes the IBM MT/ST (1964) as an early word processing machine.

questions.question: Which of these can you do easily with a word processor that is hard to do with handwriting?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists moving sentences around without rewriting as a real advantage of word processing over handwriting.
options: Move sentences around without rewriting everything

questions.question: A student says, "Word processing is basically the same as typing on an old-fashioned typewriter." What is the BEST reason this is a misconception, based on the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Typewriter Era passage explains that correcting mistakes on a typewriter meant messy correction fluid or retyping entire pages — word processors solve this by allowing easy digital editing.
options: Word processors let you easily edit, save, and reprint documents without retyping everything, unlike typewriters
Typewriters are much faster than word processors
Typewriters can save documents digitally too
Word processors cannot be used to print anything

questions.question: Sharing your work instantly with friends and teachers using just a link is a feature especially associated with:
questions.explanation: The chapter highlights that Google Docs lets you share documents with friends and teachers easily online.

questions.question: Besides Microsoft Word and Google Docs, which other program is named in the chapter as a word processing tool?
questions.explanation: The chapter mentions LibreOffice Writer alongside WordPad as other common word processing programs.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: In the chapter's Mystery Tool Challenge, which writing tool is the OLDEST, shown first in the correct order?
questions.explanation: The Mystery Tool Challenge orders the tools from oldest to newest as: quill/feather pen, typewriter, old desktop computer, tablet.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: In the chapter's Mystery Tool Challenge, which writing tool is the NEWEST, shown last in the correct order?
questions.explanation: The correct oldest-to-newest order ends with the tablet as the most modern writing tool shown.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: In the Mystery Tool Challenge's order of writing tools, which tool comes right AFTER the typewriter but BEFORE the tablet?
questions.explanation: The chapter's order is: quill/feather pen -> typewriter -> old desktop computer -> tablet.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: Around 3000 BCE, ancient writers carved symbols into:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Trail Treasure history explains that in Ancient Times (around 3000 BCE), writers carved symbols into clay tablets or stone.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: Making a change to writing on an ancient clay tablet usually meant:
questions.explanation: Since clay tablets couldn't be edited like digital text, making changes meant starting over with a new tablet.
options: Starting over with a brand new tablet

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: According to the chapter, paper was invented in:
questions.explanation: The Paper Revolution passage states paper was invented in China around 100 CE, making writing more portable.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: During the Paper Revolution, writers commonly used:
questions.explanation: The chapter describes writers using brushes, quills, and reed pens dipped in ink during the Paper Revolution era.
options: Brushes, quills, and reed pens dipped in ink

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: Correcting a mistake was easy during the Paper Revolution era.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that mistakes were difficult to correct once written with ink on paper during this era.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: The printing press, which allowed multiple copies of texts to be produced, was invented by:
questions.explanation: The chapter credits Johannes Gutenberg with inventing the printing press in the 1440s.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: What was a major drawback of making changes to text using a Gutenberg-era printing press?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that changes with a printing press required resetting heavy metal type blocks — a slow, labor-intensive process compared to modern editing.
options: It required resetting heavy metal type blocks
It used a red squiggly line to flag errors

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: The Typewriter Era described in the chapter roughly spans:
questions.explanation: The chapter's history box labels the Typewriter Era as 1870s-1960s.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: Typewriters made typing faster than handwriting.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that with mechanical typewriters, typing was faster than handwriting, though correcting errors was still difficult.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: Correcting mistakes on a mechanical typewriter typically meant:
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that fixing typewriter mistakes required messy correction fluid or retyping whole pages — unlike modern word processors.
options: Using messy correction fluid or retyping entire pages

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: The first electronic word processors (1960s-1970s) were:
questions.explanation: The chapter describes Early Word Processors (1960s-1970s) as dedicated machines, not yet full computers, that could store and edit text before printing.
options: Dedicated machines (not yet full computers) that could store text and allow editing before printing

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: Software that brought word processing to home computers in the Personal Computer Revolution (1980s) included:
questions.explanation: The chapter states that software like WordPerfect and Microsoft Word brought word processing to home computers in the 1980s.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: Programs like Google Docs, which store documents online and allow real-time collaboration, belong to which era named in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter names the Cloud Revolution (2000s-present) as the era of programs like Google Docs that store documents online.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: What is a main advantage of Cloud Revolution programs like Google Docs, per the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter highlights that Cloud Revolution programs allow access from any device and real-time collaboration with others.
options: Access from any device with real-time collaboration
They work without any internet ever

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: According to the chapter's Trail Treasure fact, the year associated with the IBM MT/ST, an early word processor, is:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Trail Treasure box associates the IBM MT/ST word processing machine with 1964.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: Douglas Engelbart is credited in the chapter with inventing:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Trail Treasure fact credits Douglas Engelbart with inventing the first computer mouse in 1964, which early word processors were among the first programs to use.

questions.topic: History of Writing Tools and Word Processors
questions.question: Which of these eras or inventions are part of the chapter's history of writing tools? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter's history traces clay tablets, paper/ink pens, the printing press, and typewriters as stages before modern word processors. Smartphone cameras are not part of this history.

questions.question: Ancient Indian manuscripts written on palm leaves are called:
questions.explanation: The Heritage Route box names ancient Indian palm-leaf manuscripts "taalapatra."

questions.question: What tool did scribes use to engrave letters onto palm leaves?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that scribes wrote on palm leaves using a pointed stylus.

questions.question: What did scribes rub into the engraved letters on palm leaves to make the writing permanent?
questions.explanation: The chapter states scribes rubbed turmeric or lamp-black paste into the engraved letters to make them permanent.

questions.question: According to the chapter, which of these are real steps in making a palm-leaf manuscript book? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter lists the five steps: Collect Palm Leaves, Dry and Smooth, Engrave with Stylus, Add Turmeric/Lamp-Black, and Bundle and Store. Printing presses are unrelated to this traditional Indian method.

questions.question: What is the FIRST step in making a palm-leaf manuscript book, per the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter lists "Collect Palm Leaves" as step 1 in the palm-leaf book-making process.

questions.question: Some palm-leaf manuscripts, over a thousand years old, are still found today in temple libraries across:
questions.explanation: The chapter states these ancient manuscripts are still found in temple libraries across Kerala, Odisha, and Tamil Nadu.

questions.question: Which ancient Indian university is said to have housed over nine million manuscripts?
questions.explanation: The Heritage Route box states Nalanda alone is said to have housed over nine million manuscripts.

questions.question: Along with Nalanda, which other ancient Indian university with a vast library is named in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter names both Nalanda and Takshashila as ancient universities with vast libraries.

questions.question: The chapter suggests that ancient Indian writing traditions have been completely lost and no manuscripts survive today.
questions.explanation: This is false — the chapter explains that manuscripts still survive in temple libraries and that India's National Mission for Manuscripts works to digitise and protect what remains.

questions.question: India's National Mission for Manuscripts works to:
questions.explanation: The chapter states this mission works to digitise and protect what remains of India's ancient manuscripts.
options: Digitise and protect remaining ancient manuscripts
Delete old manuscripts to save space
Convert manuscripts into printing press type

questions.question: According to the chapter, modern word processors support how many Indian scripts (approximately)?
questions.explanation: The chapter states word processors now support over 20 Indian scripts, including Devanagari, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali.

questions.question: Which Indian scripts are named in the chapter as supported by modern word processors? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter names Devanagari, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali as examples of the more than 20 Indian scripts supported by modern word processors.

questions.question: The Save icon in most word processors traditionally looks like a:
questions.explanation: The chapter shows the Save button icon as looking like a floppy disk.

questions.question: What were floppy discs, as mentioned in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains floppy discs were old storage devices, now replaced by pen drives and hard drives — even though the save icon still looks like one.
options: Old storage devices used to save documents, since replaced by pen drives and hard drives

questions.question: You must print your document before you can save it.
questions.explanation: This is false. The Milestone true/false activity confirms you do NOT need to print before saving — saving and printing are separate actions.

questions.question: What blinking symbol shows you where your next typed character will appear?
questions.explanation: The chapter's glossary (Guidepost 1) defines the cursor as the blinking line showing where your next character will appear.

questions.question: When creating a new document, you typically start by:
questions.explanation: Creating a document begins with opening the word processing program and starting a new/blank document before typing.
options: Opening your word processing program and choosing to start a blank/new document

questions.question: Pressing which key creates a new paragraph while typing?
questions.explanation: The chapter's worksheet and Milestone activity both confirm pressing Enter starts a new paragraph.

questions.question: Saving a file and printing a file are the same action.
questions.explanation: These are separate actions — you can save a document digitally at any time without ever printing it.

questions.question: Which keyboard shortcut is commonly used to save a document?
questions.explanation: Ctrl+S is listed in the chapter's Guidepost 1 glossary as the keyboard shortcut for Save.

questions.question: Which of the following are true about saving documents, per the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Ctrl+S is a save shortcut, the save icon resembles a floppy disk, and saving stores your work digitally. You do NOT need to print before saving.
options: The save icon often looks like a floppy disk

questions.question: A classmate says, "The floppy disk save icon means my computer still uses floppy disks." What is the best correction, based on the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains floppy discs were old storage devices, since replaced by pen drives and hard drives, even though the save icon tradition continues.
options: It's just a symbol from history; floppy disks are old technology now typically replaced by pen drives and hard drives, but the icon is still used
Floppy disks are actually a brand-new invention
The icon means you must buy a floppy disk to save
Save icons never resemble old technology

questions.question: Which of these is a digital storage device mentioned that eventually replaced floppy discs?
questions.explanation: The chapter states floppy discs were old devices replaced by pen drives and hard drives.

questions.question: Pressing Enter while typing starts a new paragraph.
questions.explanation: Confirmed by both the worksheet answer key and the Milestone true/false activity.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what should you generally do soon after starting to type a new document to avoid losing your work?
questions.explanation: Saving your document (via Ctrl+S or the save button) protects your work from being lost, as emphasized throughout the Creating and Saving Documents section.
options: Save it (using Ctrl+S or the save icon)

questions.question: Which of these best describes what happens when you click the Save button?
questions.explanation: Saving stores your document (digitally) so it can be reopened and accessed later, unlike printing which produces a paper copy.
options: Your document is stored so you can access it later
Your document is printed on paper

questions.question: According to the chapter's EcoRoute box, about what percentage of industrial wood harvested worldwide is used for paper production?
questions.explanation: The EcoRoute box states paper production uses about 40% of all industrial wood harvested globally.

questions.question: Which features of word processors help you collaborate with others WITHOUT printing or mailing paper copies?
questions.explanation: The EcoRoute box highlights Comments, Track Changes, and Sharing links as digital collaboration features that reduce the need for paper copies.
options: Comments, Track Changes, and Sharing links

questions.question: Going fully digital with documents has zero environmental impact.
questions.explanation: This is false — the chapter notes that data centres storing digital documents still consume electricity, so digital habits still carry an environmental cost.

questions.question: To be a more responsible digital citizen, the chapter suggests you should:
questions.explanation: The EcoRoute box recommends deleting unneeded files and sharing links instead of large attachments as responsible digital habits.
options: Delete unneeded files and share links instead of large attachments
Avoid using Comments or Track Changes

questions.question: The chapter's "Eco Challenge" invites students to:
questions.explanation: The Eco Challenge asks students to complete assignments digitally for a week without printing, to reduce paper use.
options: Complete assignments digitally for a week without printing
Print every assignment for a week

questions.question: Data centres that store digital documents use electricity.
questions.explanation: The chapter's EcoRoute box notes data centres consume electricity, which is why digital habits still have an environmental cost.

questions.question: Which of these are eco-friendly digital habits mentioned in the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Sharing links, deleting unneeded files, and using Track Changes/Comments are all eco-friendly habits from the chapter. Printing every draft goes against the chapter's advice to reduce paper use.
options: Share a link instead of printing/mailing copies
Delete files you no longer need
Use Track Changes/Comments instead of printing multiple drafts
Print every draft to be extra safe

questions.question: Paper production is closely linked to heavy use of which natural resource?
questions.explanation: The EcoRoute box links paper production to industrial wood harvesting.

questions.question: A student thinks, "Using Google Docs is always better for the planet than printing, no matter what." What is the more careful, balanced view suggested by the chapter's EcoRoute box?
questions.explanation: The EcoRoute box balances the paper-saving benefits of digital documents against the fact that data centres still use electricity, encouraging mindful digital habits.
options: Both have environmental costs; digital storage/sharing still needs electricity, so still be mindful of your digital habits, not just avoid paper
Printing is always better for the environment than digital documents
Digital documents have absolutely no environmental cost at all
Only paper documents use any resources

questions.question: Which feature helps reduce the need for printing multiple paper drafts of a document?
questions.explanation: Track Changes lets collaborators review edits digitally instead of printing multiple paper drafts.

questions.question: Sharing a link to a document instead of emailing a large attachment mainly helps by:
questions.explanation: The EcoRoute box recommends sharing links over large attachments as part of being a responsible digital citizen, reducing unnecessary duplicate storage.
options: Reducing duplicate copies and encouraging more responsible digital habits

questions.question: The chapter's Eco Challenge asks students to print MORE documents to practice formatting.
questions.explanation: This is false — the Eco Challenge asks students to avoid printing for a week and complete assignments digitally instead.

questions.question: Which key deletes text to the LEFT of the cursor?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains Backspace removes text to the left of the cursor, while Delete removes text to the right.

questions.question: Which key deletes text to the RIGHT of the cursor?
questions.explanation: The Delete key removes text to the right of the cursor, unlike Backspace which removes text to the left.

questions.question: Backspace and Delete do exactly the same thing.
questions.explanation: They are different: Backspace deletes text to the LEFT of the cursor, while Delete removes text to the RIGHT of the cursor.

questions.question: Which key jumps the cursor to the BEGINNING of a line?
questions.explanation: The Home key jumps the cursor to the beginning of the current line.

questions.question: Which key jumps the cursor to the END of a line?
questions.explanation: The End key jumps the cursor to the end of the current line.

questions.question: The Page Up and Page Down keys are mainly useful for:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains Page Up/Page Down help you navigate longer documents by moving through screens of content.

questions.question: Which keys move the cursor around the document, up/down/left/right?
questions.explanation: Arrow Keys are listed in the chapter as the keys used to move the cursor.

questions.question: What does the Undo button icon typically look like in a word processor?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Cyber Station 1 activity notes the Undo button looks like a curved arrow.

questions.question: Which keyboard shortcut reverses your last action?
questions.explanation: Ctrl+Z is confirmed in the chapter (and Guidepost 1) as the shortcut that reverses your last action.

questions.question: You're renaming a character throughout an entire story. What is the MOST efficient tool to use, per the chapter's Curiosity Cloud?
questions.explanation: The Curiosity Cloud explains Find and Replace is the most efficient way to change a character's name throughout an entire document.
options: Backspace, one letter at a time

questions.question: Which of these are keyboard navigation keys mentioned in the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter names Home, End, Page Up/Down, and Arrow keys as navigation keys. F1 is not mentioned as a navigation key in this chapter.

questions.question: Pressing Ctrl+Z undoes your last action.
questions.explanation: Confirmed throughout the chapter — Ctrl+Z reverses the last action taken.

questions.question: If you accidentally delete an important sentence while typing, the fastest fix per the chapter is to:
questions.explanation: Pressing Ctrl+Z immediately reverses the last action, such as an accidental deletion.

questions.question: To move the cursor to the very end of a long line of text quickly, you would press:
questions.explanation: The End key jumps the cursor straight to the end of the current line.

questions.question: Which shortcut makes text Bold?
questions.explanation: Ctrl+B is the standard keyboard shortcut for Bold, confirmed in the worksheet and Guidepost 1.

questions.question: Which shortcut makes text Italic?
questions.explanation: Ctrl+I is the standard keyboard shortcut for Italic text.

questions.question: Which shortcut Underlines text?
questions.explanation: Ctrl+U is the standard keyboard shortcut for Underline, confirmed in the Milestone matching activity.

questions.question: Bold text is best described as:
questions.explanation: The chapter and worksheet describe bold text as looking thicker and standing out.

questions.question: Italic text is best described as:
questions.explanation: The chapter describes italic text as appearing slanted to the side, created using Ctrl+I.

questions.question: Bold, Italic, and Underline are just decorations with no real purpose in a document.
questions.explanation: This is false. The chapter's Detour box explains Bold is used for emphasis/headings, Italic for titles/foreign words, and Underline traditionally for hyperlinks — each has a real purpose.

questions.question: According to the chapter, Bold formatting is especially useful for:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains Bold is especially useful for emphasis and for headings.

questions.question: Italic formatting is traditionally used for:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Detour box states italics are traditionally used for titles of books/films or foreign words.
options: Titles of books/films, or foreign words

questions.question: Underline formatting is traditionally associated with:
questions.explanation: The chapter notes underline is traditionally used to indicate hyperlinks (clickable links).

questions.question: Which of these are real text formatting options mentioned in the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Bold, Italic, and Underline are all real formatting options in the chapter. "Diagonal" is not a real formatting option mentioned.

questions.question: A student underlines a whole paragraph "just to make it look fancy." What is the best chapter-based advice?
questions.explanation: Since underline traditionally signals hyperlinks, overusing it for plain emphasis can be confusing — Bold or Italic are better suited for emphasis.
options: Underline is traditionally used for links, so it's better to use Bold or Italic for emphasis, or use underline sparingly
Underlining everything always looks more professional
Underline should replace all other formatting
Underlining has no traditional meaning at all

questions.question: Which formatting makes text thicker and darker?
questions.explanation: Bold formatting makes text thicker and darker, as confirmed in the Milestone matching activity.

questions.question: Ctrl+I applies italic formatting.
questions.explanation: Confirmed throughout the chapter — Ctrl+I is the shortcut for italic text.

questions.question: In the Milestone matching activity, "Bold" is matched with which description?
questions.explanation: The Milestone matching activity pairs Bold with the description "Makes text thicker and darker."
options: Dots or symbols for listing items

questions.question: Which of these is a font type named in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Arial is one of the font types named in the chapter, alongside Times New Roman and Comic Sans.

questions.question: Which of these are font types mentioned in the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Arial, Times New Roman, and Comic Sans are named as font types. Bold is a text formatting style, not a font type.

questions.question: Larger text sizes are especially good for:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that larger text is good for headings, helping them stand out from normal text.

questions.question: Normal body text in a document is usually around what size, per the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter states normal text is usually size 10-12, while headings use larger sizes.

questions.question: Bold is a type of font, just like Arial or Comic Sans.
questions.explanation: This is false. Bold is a text formatting style you apply to a font, not a font type itself. Arial and Comic Sans are actual font types.

questions.question: Choosing a different font mainly changes:
questions.explanation: A font is a named style of lettering, so changing fonts changes how the text visually looks.

questions.question: Which font, named in the chapter, might you choose for a fun, casual poster?
questions.explanation: Comic Sans is a font type mentioned in the chapter, often used for a fun or casual look.

questions.question: A classic, formal font often used in essays, named in the chapter, is:
questions.explanation: Times New Roman is named in the chapter's list of font types and is commonly associated with formal writing.

questions.question: You can change the font size of text in a word processor.
questions.explanation: Confirmed by the Milestone true/false activity — the false statement "You cannot change the font size" was corrected to say you CAN change it.

questions.question: A student writes their whole essay in a huge, heading-sized font. Why might the chapter's guidance suggest this is not ideal for normal body text?
questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes headings (larger text) from normal text (size 10-12), so using heading-sized text throughout an essay goes against this guidance.
options: Larger sizes are meant mainly for headings; ordinary text is usually kept around size 10-12 for readability
Word processors do not allow changing font size for body text
Larger fonts automatically fix spelling errors

questions.question: In the chapter's Milestone fill-in-the-blank activity, which word bank term relates to slanted font formatting?
questions.explanation: The Milestone fill-in-the-blank word bank includes "Italic" to complete the sentence about slanted text.

questions.question: What did Cyber Station 2 challenge students to try, regarding fonts and sizes?
questions.explanation: Cyber Station 2 in the chapter has students practice changing font size to 16, trying 3 different fonts, and combining bold and italic formatting.
options: Changing font size to 16, testing 3 fonts, and combining bold + italic
Deleting all fonts from the document

questions.question: Which alignment lines text up at the left, and is the most common alignment?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes Left alignment as the most common, with text lining up at the left.

questions.question: Which alignment is especially good for titles?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes Center alignment is good for titles, positioning text in the middle.

questions.question: Which alignment lines text up at the right side of the page?
questions.explanation: Right alignment lines all text up at the right side of the page.

questions.question: Which alignment spreads text evenly between the left and right margins?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains Justified alignment spreads text evenly between the left and right margins.

questions.question: Right alignment means all text lines up at the LEFT side of the page.
questions.explanation: This is false — the worksheet answer key corrects this statement: Right alignment means text lines up at the RIGHT side of the page.

questions.question: In Google Docs, which keyboard shortcut centers text?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes Ctrl+Shift+E is the Google Docs shortcut for center alignment.

questions.question: Which of these are real text alignment options mentioned in the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter names Left, Center, Right, and Justified as the real alignment options. "Diagonal" is not a real alignment option.

questions.question: Diagonal is NOT a real text alignment option because:
questions.explanation: The Milestone activity confirms Diagonal is the correct answer to "which of these is NOT a common text alignment option," since only Left, Center, Right, and Justified are real alignments.
options: The chapter's real alignment options are Left, Center, Right, and Justified — there is no "Diagonal" alignment
Diagonal text cannot be typed at all
Diagonal is a font, not an alignment
Diagonal is only used in tables

questions.question: Center alignment positions text in the middle of the page.
questions.explanation: Confirmed by the Milestone matching activity, which pairs Center alignment with "Positions text in the middle."

questions.question: In the Milestone matching activity, "Center alignment" was matched with which description?
questions.explanation: The Milestone matching activity pairs Center alignment with "Positions text in the middle."
options: Dots or symbols for listing items

questions.question: Which alignment would create the neat, block-like edges you often see in printed newspaper columns?
questions.explanation: Justified alignment spreads text evenly to line up both the left and right edges, giving a neat, block-like look often used in newspaper columns.

questions.question: Which alignment is generally used by default when you start typing a new document?
questions.explanation: Left alignment, being the most common, is the typical default when starting a new document.

questions.question: Which type of list uses dots or symbols to list items?
questions.explanation: A Bulleted list uses dots or symbols, as confirmed in the Milestone matching activity.

questions.question: Which type of list uses numbers and is best for steps or ordered information?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains Numbered lists are used for steps or ordered information.

questions.question: To END a list after typing your last item, you should:
questions.explanation: The chapter's list-creation steps state that pressing Enter twice ends the list.

questions.question: To add the NEXT item to a list, after typing one item, you should:
questions.explanation: Pressing Enter once moves you to the next list item, according to the chapter's steps.

questions.question: Line spacing controls:
questions.explanation: Line spacing refers to the space between lines of text in a document.
options: The space between lines of text

questions.question: Which of these are steps for creating a list, mentioned in the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter's list-creation steps are: click the bullet/number button, type your item, press Enter for the next item, and press Enter twice to end the list. Ctrl+P (Print) is unrelated.
options: Press Enter for the next item
Press Enter twice to end the list

questions.question: In the Milestone matching activity, "Bulleted list" was matched with which description?
questions.explanation: The Milestone matching activity pairs Bulleted list with "Dots or symbols for listing items."
options: Dots or symbols for listing items

questions.question: A numbered list is a good choice for showing steps in order.
questions.explanation: Numbered lists are specifically described in the chapter as best for steps or ordered information.

questions.question: Which list type would be best for a recipe's cooking steps?
questions.explanation: Since order matters for cooking steps, a Numbered list is the best fit, as the chapter explains numbered lists suit ordered information.

questions.question: Which list type would be best for a shopping list where the order doesn't matter?
questions.explanation: Bulleted lists use dots/symbols and work well when items don't need a specific order.

questions.question: Pressing Enter once at the end of your last list item will immediately end the list.
questions.explanation: This is false. According to the chapter, you need to press Enter TWICE to end a list — pressing it once just adds another list item.

questions.question: What do you click FIRST, before typing your first list item, to start a list?
questions.explanation: The chapter's list-creation steps begin with clicking the bullet/number button in the toolbar.
options: The bullet or number button in the toolbar

questions.question: To add a picture to a document, which menu do you typically use first?
questions.explanation: The chapter's steps for adding a picture begin with accessing the Insert menu.

questions.question: You can resize a picture in a document by:
questions.explanation: The worksheet answer key confirms you can resize pictures by clicking and dragging the corner handles.
options: Clicking and dragging its corner handles

questions.question: You can resize pictures in a document by clicking and dragging the corner handles.
questions.explanation: Confirmed in the worksheet's true/false answer key.

questions.question: To move a picture to a new spot in your document, you should:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains you can move a picture by clicking and dragging it to a new location.

questions.question: The feature that makes text flow neatly around a picture, instead of the picture blocking the words, is called:
questions.explanation: The chapter names Text Wrap as the feature (accessed by right-clicking a picture) that lets words flow around it.

questions.question: Once inserted, a picture's position and size can never be changed.
questions.explanation: This is false — pictures can be resized using corner handles and moved by clicking and dragging, as the chapter explains.

questions.question: In Google Docs, where do you find the option to insert an image?
questions.explanation: The chapter shows that in Google Docs, you insert an image via Insert -> Image.

questions.question: Which historical device, invented by Douglas Engelbart in 1964, is closely tied to how we interact with word processors today?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Trail Treasure fact credits Douglas Engelbart with inventing the computer mouse in 1964, which early word processors were among the first to use.

questions.question: Which of these are steps for adding a picture, per the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter's steps are: click the location, access Insert and choose Picture/Image, choose the source, then click Insert/Open. Ctrl+Z (undo) is unrelated to inserting a picture.
options: Open the Insert menu and choose picture/image

questions.question: A student's picture is stuck in the middle of a paragraph, breaking up the sentence awkwardly. Which chapter feature could fix this?
questions.explanation: Text Wrap is the feature described in the chapter for making words flow neatly around an inserted picture.
options: Text Wrap, which lets words flow around the picture

questions.question: After inserting a picture, right-clicking it usually lets you access:
questions.explanation: The chapter shows that right-clicking a picture gives access to options including Wrap Text.

questions.question: According to the chapter's Trail Treasure fact, early word processors were notable for being:
questions.explanation: The Trail Treasure fact notes early word processors were among the first programs to make use of the newly invented computer mouse.
options: Among the first computer programs to make use of the mouse
The very first typewriters ever made
Only usable with a stylus and clay tablet

questions.question: A red squiggly line under a word usually means:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Guidepost 2 glossary states a red squiggly line marks a possible spelling error.

questions.question: A blue or green squiggly line usually flags:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Guidepost 2 glossary states a blue/green squiggly line marks a possible grammar issue.

questions.question: To see spelling or grammar suggestions for a flagged word, you should:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that right-clicking a flagged word shows suggestions for correcting it.

questions.question: Spell check will catch every single grammar mistake in your document.
questions.explanation: This is false, as confirmed in the worksheet answer key — spell check and grammar check aren't perfect and may miss some errors.

questions.question: Spell check mainly identifies words that are:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Detour box explains spell check flags words not found in its dictionary, which is why it can miss correctly-spelled wrong words.

questions.question: Why might spell check MISS an error like using "there" instead of "their"?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Detour box explains spell check isn't perfect and may miss homophone-type errors since both words are technically spelled correctly.
options: Both words are spelled correctly, and spell check mainly catches misspellings, not wrong-word (homophone) errors
Spell check only works on numbers
Spell check is turned off by default
Spell check only checks the first word in a sentence

questions.question: Right-clicking a word with a red squiggly line can show you spelling suggestions.
questions.explanation: Confirmed by the chapter's explanation of how to use spell check.

questions.question: Which feature, named in the Milestone fill-in-the-blank activity, helps identify misspelled words in your document?
questions.explanation: The Milestone activity's word bank includes "Spell" to complete the sentence about the Spell check feature.

questions.question: Which of these are true about spelling and grammar checking, per the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Red squiggly = spelling, blue/green squiggly = grammar, and right-clicking shows suggestions. However, spell/grammar check is not perfect and can miss errors, so the last option is false.
options: A red squiggly line usually marks a spelling error
A blue/green squiggly line usually marks a grammar issue
It never makes mistakes and catches every error

questions.question: A student thinks, "If my document has no red or green squiggly lines, it must be 100% error-free." What's wrong with this idea?
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that spell/grammar check can miss errors such as using the wrong (but correctly spelled) homophone.
options: Spell/grammar checkers aren't perfect and can miss real errors, like correctly-spelled wrong words
Squiggly lines always appear even when there are no errors
Spell check catches every possible mistake without fail
Squiggly lines are just decorations with no meaning

questions.question: Which color squiggly line is associated with GRAMMAR issues, not spelling?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Guidepost 2 glossary confirms blue/green squiggly lines flag grammar issues.

questions.question: What should you do after right-clicking a misspelled (red-underlined) word?
questions.explanation: Right-clicking shows spelling suggestions, from which you can choose the correct spelling.
options: Choose the correct spelling from the suggestions shown
Save the document without fixing it

questions.question: Which tool locates specific text in your document?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains Find locates specific text within a document.

questions.question: Which tool finds AND changes text to something else?
questions.explanation: The chapter explains Replace finds text and changes it to something else.

questions.question: What is the keyboard shortcut for Find?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Guidepost 2 glossary lists Ctrl+F as the shortcut for Find.

questions.question: What is the keyboard shortcut for Find & Replace?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Guidepost 2 glossary lists Ctrl+H as the shortcut for Find & Replace, confirmed also on the Checkpoint 2 page.

questions.question: To change EVERY instance of a word at once, you should click:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Find and Replace steps explain that clicking Replace All changes every instance at once.

questions.question: To review and change instances of a word one at a time, you should:
questions.explanation: The chapter's steps explain clicking Find Next locates instances one by one, which you can then replace individually.
options: Click Find Next, then Replace for each one

questions.question: The Find and Replace tool can help you change a character's name throughout an entire story.
questions.explanation: Confirmed directly in the worksheet's fill-in-the-blank answer key.

questions.question: Before computers, how did authors make a consistent change (like renaming a character) throughout an entire manuscript?
questions.explanation: The chapter's Trail Treasure fact explains that before computers, authors had to read entire manuscripts by hand to make consistent changes.
options: They had to read the entire manuscript by hand to find and fix every instance
They emailed the publisher to fix it

questions.question: Which of these are steps in using Find & Replace, mentioned in the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter's 5 steps for Find & Replace include locating the tool, typing the search term, typing the replacement, and clicking Find Next/Replace. Ctrl+Z (undo) is a separate, unrelated action.
options: Look for Find/Replace in the editing menu
Type what you want to find
Type what you want to replace it with
Click Find Next or Replace All

questions.question: Find and Replace can only replace one instance of a word at a time, and never all instances at once.
questions.explanation: This is false — clicking Replace All lets you change every instance of a word at once, according to the chapter's steps.

questions.question: Which feature would you use to change all instances of "happy" to "joyful" in your document, per the Milestone activity?
questions.explanation: The Milestone activity confirms Find and Replace is the correct feature for changing every instance of one word to another.

questions.question: Which of these is the BEST reason Find and Replace is especially useful for long stories?
questions.explanation: Find and Replace saves significant time compared to manually rereading and editing a long document by hand, as historically required.
options: It saves time by automatically finding and changing every instance instead of manually rereading the whole document
It automatically adds pictures to your story
It changes the page orientation for you

questions.question: What do you need to specify FIRST when inserting a table?
questions.explanation: The worksheet answer key confirms you must specify the number of rows and columns needed first, when inserting a table.
options: The number of rows and columns needed
The text that will go inside it

questions.question: To add a table to your document, which menu do you use?
questions.explanation: The chapter's steps for creating a table begin with clicking Insert and finding Table.

questions.question: Tables organize information into:
questions.explanation: The chapter (and Milestone true/false activity) confirms tables organize information into rows and columns.

questions.question: To change a column's width in a table, you:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains you can change column width by dragging the column's border.

questions.question: To add another row or column to an existing table, you typically click:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains rows/columns can be added or deleted using the "+" sign.

questions.question: Tables help organize information into rows and columns.
questions.explanation: Confirmed by the Milestone true/false activity.

questions.question: Which is the BEST use for a table, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter states tables are perfect for schedules, comparisons, and organizing facts.
options: Organizing things like weekly schedules, comparisons, or facts

questions.question: To add text inside a table, you:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains you click inside a table cell to add text to it.
options: Click inside the cell and start typing

questions.question: Which of the following can you do with a table, per the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: You can add/delete rows and columns, change column widths, and add colours/borders to a table. Tables CAN be resized, so the last option is false.
options: Add or delete rows and columns
Only add text — you can never resize a table

questions.question: A student wants to compare 3 animals across 4 categories neatly. What is the BEST word processing feature to use?
questions.explanation: A table's rows-and-columns structure is ideal for organizing comparisons, as the chapter explains.

questions.question: Which document element uses a grid layout of rows and columns?
questions.explanation: A table uses a grid of rows and columns, per the chapter's Guidepost 2 glossary.

questions.question: Which activity in the chapter asked students to build a table for organizing days and activities?
questions.explanation: Skill Trail 3, the Weekly Schedule Creator, has students practice using tables to organize a schedule.

questions.question: The space between your text and the edge of the page is called:
questions.explanation: The Milestone activity confirms Margin is the term for the space between text and the edge of the page.

questions.question: Which page orientation is taller than it is wide?
questions.explanation: Portrait orientation is described in the chapter as taller than wide, the normal orientation for most paper.

questions.question: Which page orientation is wider than it is tall?
questions.explanation: Landscape orientation is described as wider than tall, good for tables or wide pictures.

questions.question: Which orientation would be BEST for a wide table with many columns?
questions.explanation: The worksheet confirms Landscape orientation is most suitable for displaying a wide table with many columns.

questions.question: Smaller margins let you:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains smaller margins fit more text on a page, while larger margins leave more white space.
options: Fit more text on a page

questions.question: Larger margins mean LESS white space on the page.
questions.explanation: This is false — larger margins actually mean MORE white space on the page, since more space is left between the text and the page edge.

questions.question: Page numbers can typically be added in the:
questions.explanation: The chapter explains page numbers are usually placed in the header (top) or footer (bottom) of a page.

questions.question: Portrait orientation is the normal, default orientation for most printed pages.
questions.explanation: The chapter describes Portrait as the normal orientation, taller than wide, typically used for standard printed pages.

questions.question: A student is making a document with a very wide picture that keeps getting cut off. What page setting change might help, per the chapter?
questions.explanation: Landscape orientation, being wider than tall, is better suited for wide content like large pictures or tables.

questions.question: Which of these are real page orientation options mentioned in the chapter? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Portrait and Landscape are the two real page orientation options in the chapter. Square and Vertical are not real orientation options mentioned.

questions.question: Where in a document would you typically place a page number at the very bottom?
questions.explanation: The footer, at the bottom of the page, is where page numbers are commonly placed (the header is at the top).

questions.question: Margin is best defined as:
questions.explanation: The chapter's Guidepost 1 glossary defines Margin as the white space between text and the page edge.
options: The white space between the text and the edge of the page
The space between two table columns
The blinking line where you type

questions.question: What is the MAIN advantage of word processing over handwriting, per the Milestone activity?
questions.explanation: The Milestone activity confirms the main advantage of word processing over handwriting is that it allows for easy editing and correction.
options: It allows for easy editing and correction
It is always faster, no matter what

questions.question: Word processing is better than handwriting because you can fix mistakes easily without erasing.
questions.explanation: Confirmed in the worksheet's true/false answer key.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a real advantage of word processing over handwriting?
questions.explanation: Requiring no electricity is false — word processing actually NEEDS electricity/a computer to work, unlike handwriting.
options: It requires no electricity to operate
You can move sentences around without rewriting
You can save your work digitally

questions.question: A student says, "Word processing is always faster than handwriting, no matter what." Is this the main point the chapter emphasizes?
questions.explanation: The Milestone activity specifically identifies easy editing and correction, not speed alone, as the main advantage of word processing over handwriting.
options: No — the chapter emphasizes easy EDITING and correction as the main advantage, not necessarily raw speed
Yes — speed is the only advantage mentioned
No — the chapter says handwriting is always faster
Yes — word processing is always instantly faster to set up

questions.question: Unlike handwriting, word processing lets you move sentences around:
questions.explanation: The chapter lists moving sentences around without rewriting as a real advantage of word processing.

questions.question: Handwriting makes it just as easy to fix a mistake in the middle of a page as word processing does.
questions.explanation: This is false — the whole chapter contrasts handwriting/older tools (hard to correct mistakes) with word processing, which allows easy editing and correction.

questions.question: One reason word processing can be considered better for group work is that documents can be:
questions.explanation: The chapter highlights Google Docs' ability to be shared and collaboratively edited as a benefit over handwriting.
options: Shared and edited by multiple people (e.g. using Google Docs)
Only edited by one person ever

questions.question: Which era in the chapter's history shows the SAME editing-difficulty problem as handwriting — that correcting mistakes was hard?
questions.explanation: Both the Typewriter Era (messy correction fluid/retyping) and Ancient Times (starting a new clay tablet) shared the same difficulty in correcting mistakes that handwriting has.
options: The Typewriter Era and Ancient Times (clay tablets)

questions.question: Word processing lets you print your document:
questions.explanation: Unlike handwriting, word processing lets you edit on-screen first and then print as many copies as needed.
options: As many times as needed, after editing on-screen first

questions.question: Overall, the chapter frames word processing mainly as a tool that makes writing:
questions.explanation: Across the whole chapter, word processing is presented as improving on handwriting through easier editing, correcting, formatting, saving, and sharing.
options: Easier to edit, correct, format, save, and share compared to handwriting
Only useful for typing, with no formatting options
Slower than handwriting in every case

questions.question: In the chapter's "Nutrition Junction" analogy, a document's Heading is compared to:
questions.explanation: The Nutrition Junction infographic compares a large, bold Heading to Complex Carbohydrates, the main energy that anchors a page.

questions.question: In the Nutrition Junction analogy, Body Text (regular) is compared to:
questions.explanation: Body Text (regular) is compared to Proteins — steady builders keeping concentration going through a long document.

questions.question: In the Nutrition Junction analogy, Bullet Points are compared to:
questions.explanation: Bullet Points are compared to Vegetables & Fruits — each one a quick burst of vitamins, like a colourful bullet point.

questions.question: In the Nutrition Junction analogy, White Space/Margins are compared to:
questions.explanation: White Space/Margins are compared to Water — the "empty space" a document (like your body) cannot work without.

questions.question: In the Nutrition Junction analogy, the Ctrl+Z (Undo) shortcut is compared to:
questions.explanation: Ctrl+Z (Undo) is compared to Sleep — the overnight "undo" that repairs the day's errors and consolidates memory.

questions.question: In the Nutrition Junction analogy, Bullet Points are compared to Proteins.
questions.explanation: This is false — Bullet Points are compared to Vegetables & Fruits, while Proteins are compared to Body Text (regular).

questions.question: Which of these are correct analogy pairs from the chapter's Nutrition Junction infographic? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The correct pairs are Heading=Carbohydrates, Body Text=Proteins, and Margins=Water. Bullet Points are compared to Vegetables & Fruits, not Sleep (Sleep is paired with Ctrl+Z/Undo).

questions.question: Why does the chapter compare the Ctrl+Z (Undo) shortcut to sleep?
questions.explanation: The Nutrition Junction infographic explains sleep is like an overnight "undo" for the body, paralleling how Ctrl+Z reverses a mistake in a document.
options: Because sleep is described as the overnight "undo" that repairs the day's errors and consolidates memory, just like Ctrl+Z reverses a mistake
Because sleep and Ctrl+Z both delete your document
Because you must sleep before you can undo anything
Because Ctrl+Z only works while you are asleep

questions.question: Which shortcut is used to Save a document, per the chapter's Guidepost glossary?
questions.explanation: Guidepost 1 lists Ctrl+S as the shortcut for Save.

questions.question: Which key, in Microsoft Word, is listed as a shortcut for Spell Check, per Guidepost 2?
questions.explanation: Guidepost 2 lists F7 as the Microsoft Word shortcut for Spell Check.

questions.question: You CAN change the font size of text in a word processor.
questions.explanation: Confirmed by the Milestone true/false activity, which corrects the false statement "You cannot change the font size."

questions.question: Which of these is the correct keyboard shortcut PAIR, according to Guidepost 2?
questions.explanation: Guidepost 2 lists Ctrl+F for Find and Ctrl+H for Find & Replace.

questions.question: In the Milestone true/false section, the false statement "You cannot change the font size of text in a word processor" should be corrected to say:
questions.explanation: Since the original statement is false, the correction is that you CAN in fact change the font size of text.
options: You CAN change the font size of text in a word processor
You can never change any formatting
Font size can only be changed by an adult

questions.question: In the Milestone fill-in-the-blank word bank (floppy disk, Italic, cursor, Spell), which word completes "Text that is ___ appears slanted"?
questions.explanation: "Italic" correctly completes the sentence about slanted text in the Milestone activity's word bank.

questions.question: In the Milestone matching activity, "Underline" is matched with:
questions.explanation: The Milestone matching activity pairs Underline with the shortcut Ctrl+U.
options: Dots or symbols for listing items

questions.question: According to the Milestone true/false section, you must print a document before you're able to save it.
questions.explanation: This is false — the Milestone activity confirms you do NOT need to print before saving; they are separate actions.

questions.question: Which glossary term from Guidepost 1 means "the white space between text and the edge of the page"?
questions.explanation: Guidepost 1 defines Margin as the white space between text and the page edge.

questions.question: Which glossary term from Guidepost 2 describes "a grid of rows and columns for organising information"?
questions.explanation: Guidepost 2 defines Table as a grid of rows and columns for organising information.
